headline: “Possible” is “may” plus “able” — borrowed whole from Middle Chinese.
A memory is a “thought” that has “come out”.
Lunch, or noon, is a beautified “daytime”.
A serious face may be one with nervous, blinking eyes — and the kanji only fake the logic.
A crowd got its おお from native Japanese, grafted onto a Chinese word.
ナンバー has a twin in Japanese: ノンブル.
“Nostalgic” first meant wanting to keep something close — and only later became about remembering.
To change clothes is to “put on” and “exchange” — with the かえる voicing to がえる.
“Effort” is, in Chinese, “to exert strength”.
“Docile” is “adult” plus an adjective-forming ending.
To betray is to “cut” the “back” — きる voiced to ぎる.
“To think” has a long run of sound changes from kamugapu, and a handful of rival theories for its start.
“Two days” has a ふつ that is not the usual reading of 二.
The organ travelled as an “internationalism”, so its immediate source is hard to pin down.
To tell is to “narrate a thing” — with かたる voiced to がたる.
A hint or sign is a “mood crawling around” — spelled with a 配 that was only fitted to the sound.
In its older native reading, “young girl” was “little” plus “female” — much as the word for “man” began as “young boy”.
“Considerable” is “big” plus a verb that says it's already done.
The checkout is a clipped “register”.
“Wonderful” began as “that which makes one shrink away” — a strongly negative word.
A jacket is “upper wear”, using a bound form of “up” and a voiced ぎ.
A zabuton is a “seat futon”, with ふとん voicing to ぶとん.
To till a field began as a “field” plus “return”, and the middle of the word has since softened.
The “however” that opens a caveat is a “just” with an emphatic particle on the end.
“Nutrition” was spelled two ways until a 1920 institute and a 1926 publication settled it.
“Always” is “constancy” with an adverbial に on the end.
Papa could be English, or German — nobody can say which.
“To be visible” began as “see” with a suffix that means “can be”.
A boy is a “male child” with a little の in between, first cited in 1711.
A tatami room was named for sitting mats long before tatami floors were common.
